a3080.speech: Told the Reuters news agency that they were expecting China’s military to display a host of new weaponry and equipment at the parade, including military trucks fitted with devices to take out drones, new tanks and early warning aircraft to protect China’s aircraft carriers.

a3123.speaker: Ayalew Addis, Ethiopian businessperson and co-owner of BeligoEth Plc
a3123.name: Ayalew Addis
a3123.title: Ethiopian businessperson and co-owner of BeligoEth Plc
a3123.speech: According to Ayalew, the factory requires a small labour force as it will be semi-automated.

a3123.speaker: Ayalew Addis, Ethiopian businessperson and co-owner of BeligoEth Plc
a3123.name: Ayalew Addis
a3123.title: Ethiopian businessperson and co-owner of BeligoEth Plc
a3123.speech: “The design was sent to our European partners for review,” Ayalew told Fortune. “We will be floating a tender next month to hire a construction company.”

a3123.speaker: Ayalew Addis, Ethiopian businessperson and co-owner of BeligoEth Plc
a3123.name: Ayalew Addis
a3123.title: Ethiopian businessperson and co-owner of BeligoEth Plc
a3123.speech: According to Ayalew, upon being fully operational in three years, the company plans to substitute its own products for imports and export its products to other East African countries.

a3123.speaker: Ayalew Addis, Ethiopian businessperson and co-owner of BeligoEth Plc
a3123.name: Ayalew Addis
a3123.title: Ethiopian businessperson and co-owner of BeligoEth Plc
a3123.speech: According to Ayalew, the company chose Debre Berhan for the investment after considering the weather of Chacha wereda, one of the 24 rural weredas in North Shoa. “The chemicals and the products need to be stored at a cold temperature,” Ayalew said.

a3123.speaker: Tadele Minda, director of the wereda’s land use and management office
a3123.name: Tadele Minda
a3123.title: director of the wereda’s land use and management office
a3123.speech: According to Tadele, the area is getting more investment these days. “Besides, the area is preferable for agro-processing,” Tadele told Fortune.

a3123.speaker: Beteley Tekola (PhD), consultant and academic in chemical engineering
a3123.name: Beteley Tekola (PhD)
a3123.title: consultant and academic in chemical engineering
a3123.speech: “The chemical industry is at its infant stage. Therefore, investors should get support from the government.”

a3151.speaker: Chiefs and village leaders (Kasungu)
a3151.name: Chiefs and village leaders (Kasungu)
a3151.speech: Described the gesture [Chithyola’s donation of 6,000 bags of maize worth K21 million to vulnerable households] as “life-saving” at a time when hunger was widespread.

a3151.speaker: European Union
a3151.name: European Union
a3151.speech: Praised the 2024/25 budget as “a budget full of hope.”

a3151.speaker: World Bank
a3151.name: World Bank
a3151.speech: Commended Malawi’s “incredible economic results” under his stewardship.

a3326.speaker: Myriam Montrat, Canadian High Commissioner to Ghana
a3326.name: Myriam Montrat
a3326.title: Canadian High Commissioner to Ghana
a3326.speech: Has stressed the African Continental Free Trade Agreement's (AfCFTA) capacity to enable economies to scale and position Africa as a more competitive player in global value chains; said its success depends on translating policy goals into tangible business support systems: "AfCFTA provides a unique platform to now further reduce trade barriers and harmonise regulations. It also provides a platform to enable economies of scale and position Africa as a more competitive player in global value chains. However, unlocking its full benefits will require bridging the gap between policy and practice. It has to ensure that entrepreneurs have the tools, the financing, and market intelligence to be able to seize cross-border opportunities." (in a speech read on her behalf by Senior Trade Commissioner Andrew Maharaj)

a3326.speaker: Myriam Montrat, Canadian High Commissioner to Ghana
a3326.name: Myriam Montrat
a3326.title: Canadian High Commissioner to Ghana
a3326.speech: Affirmed Canada's commitment to deepening trade and investment ties with Africa in three key ways - business-to-business connections facilitated by the Trade Commissioner Service, partnerships with local business associations, and development cooperation supporting private sector growth: "Canadian companies are actively collaborating with African partners. We have multiple projects across renewable energy projects, responsible mining, innovative agri-tech solutions that not only scale businesses but also deliver value and social and environmental benefits. I'm particularly pleased by Canada's funding of $19.7 million over four years to the trademark Africa-led project titled: Making Trade Work for Women in West Africa. This funding, in partnership with AfCFTA Secretariat as well as ECOWAS Secretariat, is improving trade across the board of six countries in West Africa, namely Burkina Faso, Ghana, Cote d'Ivoire, Togo, Guinea, and Nigeria."

a3326.speaker: Myriam Montrat, Canadian High Commissioner to Ghana
a3326.name: Myriam Montrat
a3326.title: Canadian High Commissioner to Ghana
a3326.speech: Urged African entrepreneurs to view Canadian companies as innovation partners rather than merely suppliers or investors, highlighting their global expertise, long-term commitment, and respect for local knowledge; further encouraged foreign companies to engage with Africa's integrated market, describing the opportunities as real and the potential as vast.

a3326.speaker: Julius Debrah, Chief of Staff at the Office of the President of Ghana
a3326.name: Julius Debrah
a3326.title: Chief of Staff at the Office of the President of Ghana
a3326.speech: Explained that government would maintain strict fiscal discipline while channeling investments into critical growth sectors, and said such measures were essential to protecting growth momentum and strengthening Ghana's competitiveness in regional and global markets: "Our government continues to prioritise trade facilitation and infrastructure to ease the movement of goods and services across borders, macroeconomic stability, and reforms to ensure that Ghana remains a safe and attractive investment destination."

a3326.speaker: Mohammed Adam Sukparu, Deputy Minister for Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations
a3326.name: Mohammed Adam Sukparu
a3326.title: Deputy Minister for Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations
a3326.speech: Emphasised the pivotal role of technology in advancing Africa's economic integration under the AfCFTA; stressed the need for Africa to transition from being a consumer of technology to a producer and innovator, which he said required robust collaboration between governments, the private sector, and academia; urged entrepreneurs to adopt digital tools and investors to deepen partnerships with Africa's growing tech ecosystem; affirmed the Ministry's commitment to driving digital transformation across the continent: "the future of Africa's business lies not just in its markets, but in its innovation. If we digitize Africa, we globalize Africa."

a3528.speaker: Florent Kpatindé, consultant-trainer in international trade and specialist in business support
a3528.name: Florent Kpatindé
a3528.title: consultant-trainer in international trade and specialist in business support
a3528.speech: “Complying with international manufacturing standards facilitates access to foreign markets”; said international trade through exporting can contribute to a country’s development by attracting more investment and can allow entrepreneurs, producer groups and service providers to increase their sales opportunities, but that many companies already thriving locally with innovative, exportable products hesitate to sell abroad, among other reasons because of a lack of knowledge of the international trade environment.

a3528.speaker: Florent Kpatindé, consultant-trainer in international trade
a3528.name: Florent Kpatindé
a3528.title: consultant-trainer in international trade
a3528.speech: Said reasons for a company to consider exporting include the need to develop the business by diversifying its clientele and increasing sales volume, to be less dependent on the local market and protected against fluctuations in domestic demand, to increase output, productivity and competitiveness through improved products, production processes and staff performance, and to earn foreign currency thanks to higher profit margins on international markets; said the entrepreneur wishing to export should know the standards of international trade and their sources of information in order to seize business opportunities and manage strategies more successfully, and that companies whose leaders adapt their strategy to the requirements of international trade will prosper.

a3528.speaker: Florent Kpatindé, consultant-trainer in international trade
a3528.name: Florent Kpatindé
a3528.title: consultant-trainer in international trade
a3528.speech: Said the challenges facing companies engaged in international trade include the considerable number of standards to comply with, the capacity to adapt to market fluctuations, fierce competition, and invisible barriers blocking access to value chains; added that a company must also take into account the adaptation of existing products to market needs, the improvement of staff techniques and know-how, the search for new capital, long-term investment of resources combined with patience before a return on investment, the political, financial and legal framework of the importing country, shipping distances and transport questions, and the inability to order in bulk because of certain obstacles.

a3528.speaker: Florent Kpatindé, consultant-trainer in international trade
a3528.name: Florent Kpatindé
a3528.title: consultant-trainer in international trade
a3528.speech: Said international trade regulation can hinder or facilitate a company’s exports, requiring investment of time, funds and effort in complying with visible and invisible barriers; said potential exporters must stay informed of global trade changes and ensure their internal or external legal services master the laws in force in other countries, because despite the standardisation efforts of the WTO — “the only international organisation legislating between nations in matters of trade” — legal divergences still exist between countries on intellectual property, copyright, patents and trademarks, sanitary regulation, environmental protection laws, public standards, import conditions and taxes, labelling language, consumer protection and international payment conditions.

a3528.speaker: Florent Kpatindé, consultant-trainer in international trade
a3528.name: Florent Kpatindé
a3528.title: consultant-trainer in international trade
a3528.speech: Said countries require imported goods to comply with internationally required quality, wholesomeness and safety standards, which allow buyers to verify quality and specifications and which protect consumer health and safety and the environment; said complying with international manufacturing standards facilitates access to foreign markets, that these standards change and exporters must stay in contact with national standardisation bodies for the latest information, and that when an SME’s production processes do not respect the standards of the importing country its products will run up against trade barriers, regulations possibly requiring testing in the importing country or stricter and more costly tests than for local competing products — a practice that would be “quite taxing” for SMEs in developing countries like Benin.

a3528.speaker: Florent Kpatindé, consultant-trainer in international trade
a3528.name: Florent Kpatindé
a3528.title: consultant-trainer in international trade
a3528.speech: Said exporters must ensure their products or services conform to the target market’s standards through certification testing, product approval in the importing country, and quality-management certification; said companies must also master the agreements and treaties governing international trade — the WTO agreements guaranteeing trade rights to member countries, the GATT treaties, the GATS agreements on services and the TRIPS agreement on intellectual property, under which each country should revise its laws to better protect patents and other forms of intellectual property.

a3528.speaker: Florent Kpatindé, consultant-trainer in international trade
a3528.name: Florent Kpatindé
a3528.title: consultant-trainer in international trade
a3528.speech: Observed that, independently of the legal efforts an exporter must make, some of the greatest difficulties faced by exporters from developing countries are encountered at the border of their own country of origin, notably compliance with visible and invisible barriers, the cost of that compliance and the expenses of adapting the exporting SME’s activities to the changes those barriers induce.

a3622.speaker: John Dramani Mahama, NDC flagbearer and former President of Ghana
a3622.name: John Dramani Mahama
a3622.title: NDC flagbearer and former President of Ghana
a3622.speech: In remarks at the NDC manifesto launch in Winneba, said: “Today, we gather with hope as one people, united in victory, and as one nation – Ghana – with a common, interwoven, indivisible destiny... A destiny that cannot afford to endure one additional day beyond January 7, 2025, of the maladministration, mismanagement, and state capture this nation has been subjected to over the last almost 8 years. My brothers and sisters, Ghana is bleeding. Ghana’s soul is crying for change! Mother Ghana is crying for its true and genuine patriotic citizens to rise to reset our beloved nation. Ghanaians can take no more of the hardship, impunity, state capture, hypocrisy, lies, and bad governance inflicted over the two terms of this outgoing administration. We cannot fail Mother Ghana. Therefore, I urge you to vote for CHANGE on December 7.” ; “Your vote on December 7 will end tyranny, cronyism, corruption, and hardship. It will also pave the way for the vision, experience, and trustworthiness I, John Dramani Mahama, will restore to the Flagstaff House. As I have said before, this government must begin writing their handing-over notes if they have not done so already. This NPP administration has been the biggest political scam pulled on Ghanaians since our independence in 1957... most Ghanaians will agree that Nana Akufo-Addo is indeed the President Ghana never got. Indeed, I daresay, his much-touted economic whizz kid Dr. Mahamoud Bawumia is also the economic messiah Ghana never got.”

a3622.speaker: John Dramani Mahama, NDC flagbearer and former President of Ghana
a3622.name: John Dramani Mahama
a3622.title: NDC flagbearer and former President of Ghana
a3622.speech: Listed what the NPP government inherited from his administration on January 7, 2017: an energy sector stabilised with the fastest mobilisation of emergency power of almost 800 megawatts; a new Energy Sector Levy Act (ESLA) with potential revenues of GH¢3 billion per annum; an ongoing Millennium Challenge Compact of $547 million aimed at making Ghana’s energy sector the most efficient in Africa — noting that “the family’s quarrel over shares in the PDS company led to the US pulling back $190 million, which was meant for the most critical component of the compact, private sector participation and improvement in collections at the distribution end of the electricity value chain”; more than $450 million of the IMF Extended Credit Facility; cocoa production of 964,000 metric tons; two new oil-producing fields, TEN and ENI; a stabilisation fund of $277 million, a Ghana Infrastructure Investment Fund with seed money of $270 million and a sinking fund with over $200 million; a budget deficit of 6.1% with zero Central Bank borrowing; a currency at about GH¢4 to USD1; inflation at 15.4%, unemployment at 8.4% and debt at 57% of GDP; and an economy set to grow at above 8% as predicted by the World Bank, IMF, and all the credit rating agencies.

a3622.speaker: John Dramani Mahama, NDC flagbearer and former President of Ghana
a3622.name: John Dramani Mahama
a3622.title: NDC flagbearer and former President of Ghana
a3622.speech: Said the scorecard of the administration has been abysmal: inflation that went as high as 54% and is currently hovering above 20%; one of the highest food inflation rates in Africa; a currency that has depreciated to almost GH¢16 to USD1; over GH¢70 billion borrowed from the BOG; debt to GDP as high as 104% and unemployment at almost 15%; default on debts and a debt exchange with painful haircuts; plummeting cocoa production and a COCOBOD syndication with no takers, delayed delivery of almost 350,000 tons and default on almost GH¢13 billion in cocoa bonds; oil and gas production down 32%; massive SOE losses; and a COVID windfall of almost GH¢25 billion “most of which was doled out to companies owned by family and relatives.” He added: “Corruption is at its highest and Ghanaians are numb to the scandals that are exposed almost every week. And when you have a President who says he does not understand the hullaballoo about the sale of SSNIT hotels to a minister in his government, then clearly, he is on a completely different wavelength than the rest of the country. This is a President who doesn’t get it!”

a3622.speaker: John Dramani Mahama, NDC flagbearer and former President of Ghana
a3622.name: John Dramani Mahama
a3622.title: NDC flagbearer and former President of Ghana
a3622.speech: Invoked the Parable of the Talents (Matthew 25:14-30): “In the case of Akufo Addo/Bawumia and their cabal, they did not bury the talents given to them by the people of Ghana and return them to us. They gambled with the talents we gave them and landed the people of Ghana in a huge debt.” He argued that “a vote for the NPP will be an expression of satisfaction with the impunity of the last 8 years... a vote to allow officials who have raped this country’s resources to escape accountability,” and that “our nation needs a reset! Our democracy needs a reset! Our economy needs a reset! Our governance needs a reset. Our attitudes need a reset!”

a3622.speaker: John Dramani Mahama, NDC flagbearer and former President of Ghana
a3622.name: John Dramani Mahama
a3622.title: NDC flagbearer and former President of Ghana
a3622.speech: Presented highlights of the NDC manifesto: a National Economic Dialogue in the first 120 days to draw up a 4-year fiscal consolidation programme; rationalising taxes and abolishing the E-levy, COVID levy and 10% levy on bet winnings; emergency measures to stabilise the cedi; investigating the Gold-for-Oil deal; a no-academic-fee policy for first years in public tertiary institutions, free tertiary education for PWDs and free sanitary pads; uncapping the National Health Insurance Levy and establishing the Ghana Medical Care Trust (MahamaCares) Fund for chronic diseases; a 24-Hour Economy on a 1:3:3 formula; an Accelerated Export Development Council; a Women’s Development Bank to empower one million Ghanaian women; a National Apprenticeship Programme and free technical and vocational training; the “Adwumawura” start-up programme; a Digital Jobs Initiative with $3 billion in private investment and a One Million Coders Programme; rapid industrialisation and agriculture-for-jobs programmes; reducing government to sixty ministers, scrapping ex gratia and waging a “Ruthless War Against Corruption: Operation-Recover-All-Loot (ORAL)”, including reopening investigations into the Ayawaso West Wuogon by-election violence, the 2020 election killings and the murders of Ahmed Hussein-Suale and Silas Wulochamey; education reforms including improving Free SHS and abolishing the teacher licensure examination; modern railways; and responsible mining measures including banning new mining leases in forest reserves, a Ghana Gold Board (GOLDBOD), a ‘Tree for Life’ re-forestation policy and a Blue Water Initiative.

a3652.speaker: Professor Charles Anosike, Director General and CEO of the Nigerian Meteorological Agency (NiMet) and Permanent Representative of Nigeria with the WMO
a3652.name: Professor Charles Anosike
a3652.title: Director General and CEO of the Nigerian Meteorological Agency (NiMet) and Permanent Representative of Nigeria with the WMO
a3652.speech: Has said that effective early warning system, equipping farmers with the knowledge of weather patterns and seasonal forecasting could boost food security and ensure adequate protection from climate disasters ; said that Nigeria is presently facing food security challenges which requires a new way of thinking by integrating weather and climate related factors into the entire agricultural value chain ; “NiMet is working with partners to mainstream weather and climate information in the agricultural value chain. We are using co-production mechanism to facilitate our seasonal climate prediction. NiMet ensures appropriate understanding and use of weather information by stakeholders to improve planning and strategic decision making. Our annual Seasonal Climate Prediction (SCP) is a climate action -early warning tool that gives an outlook of weather and climate variability in upcoming months within the year. It highlights rainfall patterns and temperature variability” ; “Unpredictable rainfall patterns and extreme events can trigger competition for food and water. Declining agricultural outputs can lead to loss of income and exacerbate food insecurity. Temperature changes affect crop growth and yield, and can also destroy crops during post processing and transportation” ; “We need to intensify our collaborative efforts with deliberate and intentional strategy to promote climate-smart agriculture and invest in preparedness, and improve the response ability of our smallholder farmers. Climate change may not be the only source of our problems, however, climate change is the ‘threat multiplier’ as it intensifies resource scarcity and deepens food insecurity.”

a3693.speaker: United Nations Secretary-General (2024 report on the implementation of the Global Compact for Safe, Orderly and Regular Migration)
a3693.name: United Nations Secretary-General (2024 report on the implementation of the Global Compact for Safe
a3693.title: Orderly and Regular Migration)
a3693.speech: A report issued in New York today by the United Nations Secretary-General recommends concrete steps to reduce the risk that migrants die or go missing, including the need to provide access to humanitarian actors to deliver assistance to those in distress and improve data collection about those who are missing ; introduces key recommendations on providing humanitarian assistance to migrants in distress and strengthening cooperation on missing migrants, including concrete proposals to prevent migrants from dying or going missing, enhance search and identification efforts, support affected families, provide justice, accountability and redress, collect data on migrant deaths and disappearances and share migration forecasting data to optimize humanitarian assistance.

a3693.speaker: 2024 report on the implementation of the Global Compact for Safe, Orderly and Regular Migration (GCM)
a3693.name: 2024 report on the implementation of the Global Compact for Safe
a3693.title: Orderly and Regular Migration (GCM)
a3693.speech: Recognizes that significant strides have been made in recent years, such as integrating migration into national development plans and the expansion of safe and regular pathways for migration; however, it underscores persistent and severe challenges that demand urgent attention — irregular migration routes continue to expose migrants to grave risks, many migrants face barriers to accessing essential services, and harmful narratives and stereotypes about migration and migrants undermine efforts to protect their dignity and rights ; introduces a new voluntary framework of indicators providing a roadmap for evaluating GCM implementation, and urges Member States to adopt these indicators in their national GCM reviews, implement the actionable recommendations, and actively participate in regional reviews.

a3693.speaker: Amy Pope, International Organization for Migration Director General and coordinator of the United Nations Network on Migration
a3693.name: Amy Pope
a3693.title: International Organization for Migration Director General and coordinator of the United Nations Network on Migration
a3693.speech: “Each one of these deaths is a preventable tragedy” ; “This GCM report lays out specific, and much needed, steps to save lives and protect the rights of migrants.”

a3769.speaker: Henry Muhongo, State prosecutor
a3769.name: Henry Muhongo
a3769.title: State prosecutor
a3769.speech: "I am of the view that this application is of people who do not want to take accountability and appreciate their own wrongdoing." ; Argued in the High Court that the group comprising Mamsy Nuuyoma, Isaac Cupessala, Paquete Americano Jose, Aurelio Miapia and Noah 'Boykie' Naukosho have no prospect of succeeding should the High Court grant them leave to appeal their convictions and sentence in the Supreme Court ; explained the court did not misdirect itself when it convicted and subsequently sentenced all 14 men and women on various counts of fraud, alternatively theft, money laundering and corruptly giving a document containing false information to an agent ; said compared to similar cases, the court was lenient by imposing sentences ranging from 14 to two years respectively, and thus the group's application has no merit and stands to be dismissed.

a3769.speaker: Trevor Brockerhoff, lawyer for Naukosho, Miapia, Cupessala and Jose
a3769.name: Trevor Brockerhoff
a3769.title: lawyer for Naukosho, Miapia, Cupessala and Jose
a3769.speech: "The court erred in law and fact by finding that documentary evidence relied upon to convict was properly before court, and convicted them on some counts where some of the witnesses relevant to those counts did not testify."

a3769.speaker: Winnie Christians, lawyer for Nuuyoma
a3769.name: Winnie Christians
a3769.title: lawyer for Nuuyoma
a3769.speech: Said the search and seizure was not in accordance with the law and the court relied on circumstantial evidence to convict the group; that the State allegedly failed to present a case which proved the guilt of Nuuyoma and others beyond reasonable doubt, and thus another court if presented with the same facts might give a different conclusion.

a3986.speaker: U.S. Embassy in Addis Ababa (statement)
a3986.name: U.S. Embassy in Addis Ababa (statement)
a3986.speech: Announced that the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) will continue its programs in Ethiopia under a new structure ; said the programs, which include USAID's regional operations, will focus on humanitarian aid, health, and food security, conducted under a new bilateral assistance agreement reached between the U.S. State Department and the government of Ethiopia ; explained that this realignment, enacted under President Trump and Secretary Rubio, aims to better serve U.S. national interests through foreign assistance ; “This transition was designed to reduce duplication, strengthen accountability, and better align assistance programs with U.S. foreign policy and national security objectives” ; stated that USAID's regional operations will also transition to corresponding State Department bureaus, ensuring a continued focus on regionally responsive aid delivery, as part of a broader initiative to streamline the worldwide delivery of life-saving assistance.

a3986.speaker: Ervin Massinga, U.S. Ambassador to Ethiopia
a3986.name: Ervin Massinga
a3986.title: U.S. Ambassador to Ethiopia
a3986.speech: Earlier signaled that the majority of U.S. assistance on healthcare, agriculture, and for internally displaced persons (IDPs) would be resumed.

a4126.speaker: UN Human Rights Office
a4126.name: UN Human Rights Office
a4126.speech: Cited as the source that gang-related violence has caused nearly 4,000 deaths in 2024.

a4126.speaker: Grégoire Goodstein, IOM’s Chief of Mission in Haiti
a4126.name: Grégoire Goodstein
a4126.title: IOM’s Chief of Mission in Haiti
a4126.speech: “The isolation of Port-au-Prince is amplifying an already dire humanitarian situation” ; “Our ability to deliver aid is stretched to its limits. Without immediate international support, the suffering will worsen exponentially. With only 20 percent of Port-au-Prince accessible, humanitarian workers face immense challenges in reaching affected populations.”

a4126.speaker: International Organization for Migration (IOM) (statement distributed by African Media Agency)
a4126.name: International Organization for Migration (IOM) (statement distributed by African Media Agency)
a4126.speech: Emphasizes the critical importance of upholding humanitarian principles amid the escalating crisis, stating that ensuring the safety and security of humanitarian personnel and civilians is paramount, and calls on all to respect the neutrality and impartiality of aid operations, allowing unimpeded access to those in need and safeguarding the integrity of humanitarian assistance.

a4126.speaker: International Organization for Migration (IOM) (statement distributed by African Media Agency)
a4126.name: International Organization for Migration (IOM) (statement distributed by African Media Agency)
a4126.speech: Further calls to urgently increase funding and support for humanitarian operations in Haiti, noting that as of November the UN’s $674 million response plan remains only 42 per cent funded, leaving millions of Haitians without the assistance they desperately need.

a4313.speaker: United Nations humanitarian agency
a4313.name: United Nations humanitarian agency
a4313.speech: Expressed its deep concern at the deterioration of the security situation in Sudan, in particular the attacks against displaced persons and humanitarian workers.

a4313.speaker: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
a4313.name: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
a4313.speech: Reported on Thursday that thousands of displaced people had fled Zamzam for El-Fasher, taking refuge in open spaces and abandoned houses.

a4313.speaker: Clémentine Nkweta-Salami, UN humanitarian coordinator for Sudan
a4313.name: Clémentine Nkweta-Salami
a4313.title: UN humanitarian coordinator for Sudan
a4313.speech: Denounced the attacks and the blocking of the evacuation routes, stressing that the wounded were not receiving care ; “I am shocked by the attacks against the Zamzam displacement camp and the blocking of the evacuation routes, which endanger the lives of civilians, while the wounded are not being treated,” she deplored on X.

a4313.speaker: United Nations
a4313.name: United Nations
a4313.speech: Called for an urgent de-escalation of the conflict, stressing the need for unrestricted humanitarian space to respond to the needs of millions of vulnerable people; denounced the restrictions imposed by the Sudanese Agency for Relief and Humanitarian Operations (SARHO), associated with the RSF, which impede the delivery of vital aid.

a4313.speaker: United Nations (displacement figures)
a4313.name: United Nations (displacement figures)
a4313.speech: According to the UN, Sudan is now the scene of the largest forced displacement crisis in the world, with nearly 9 million people displaced within the country and 3.5 million having fled to neighbouring countries since the conflict began in April 2023.

a4313.speaker: International Organization for Migration (IOM)
a4313.name: International Organization for Migration (IOM)
a4313.speech: According to the IOM, around 8,000 families have been displaced from the village of Saloma after an attack attributed to the paramilitaries.

a4313.speaker: World Health Organization (WHO)
a4313.name: World Health Organization (WHO)
a4313.speech: Warned about the attacks against health facilities, having recorded 13 attacks in less than 40 days, causing 79 deaths and 59 injuries; stressed that Sudan accounts for more than 20% of the attacks against health care in the world in 2025.

a4392.speaker: Heineken consumer met in a Bujumbura bar (anonymous)
a4392.name: Heineken consumer met in a Bujumbura bar (anonymous)
a4392.speech: "We are entitled to protection like all other consumers. The government must get its act together" ; complains that since December 2019 bar owners keep charging top prices and that sellers of the 33 cl Heineken are engaging in outrageous speculation: "In four months, it is frustrating to see that the price of beer has gone up by more than 50%" ; says the increase is exaggerated and unjustified.

a4392.speaker: Other consumers (anonymous)
a4392.name: Other consumers (anonymous)
a4392.speech: Deplore the silence of the Minister of Trade, who is responsible for regulating prices, and say the government should make sure traders respect the profit margin set by law.

a4392.speaker: Bar owner in Gihosha (anonymous retailer)
a4392.name: Bar owner in Gihosha (anonymous retailer)
a4392.speech: Says that "suppliers have raised their prices" and accuses wholesalers of the increase ; stresses the shortage was not caused by the Covid-19 pandemic but began in December 2019: "A case of 24 bottles has gone from 75,000 to 120,000 BIF. We are forced to raise the price of a bottle to keep our profit margin." ; says wholesalers enjoy a monopoly, with a group of five people holding an import licence: "You understand why they call the shots." ; says the shortage and price rise are hurting his profits: "Our clientele has dropped sharply. It is a big loss. Before, I could easily sell 300 cases a week." and admits he is currently operating at a loss.

a4392.speaker: Melchiade Niyonzima, official of DIGITI (a licensed importer of Heineken)
a4392.name: Melchiade Niyonzima
a4392.title: official of DIGITI (a licensed importer of Heineken)
a4392.speech: Says his company has not raised prices: "We sell the case at 76,000 BIF." ; states the company sells the beer with full transparency: "We send the list and the invoices of the customers served to the Minister of Trade", and specifies that monitoring whether customers respect prices is the Minister of Trade's role ; points out that since January the company has recorded delivery delays because of the Covid-19 pandemic, with borders sometimes closed or suppliers lengthening delivery times.

a4392.speaker: Amstel bock drinker (anonymous consumer)
a4392.name: Amstel bock drinker (anonymous consumer)
a4392.speech: "It is a disgrace. Traders raise the price by more than 150% in full view of the commercial representatives" ; wonders where the Ministry of Trade inspectors responsible for enforcing prices have gone.

a4392.speaker: Pierre Nduwayo, president of Abuco (Burundian Consumers Association)
a4392.name: Pierre Nduwayo
a4392.title: president of Abuco (Burundian Consumers Association)
a4392.speech: "Traders push up the prices of Heineken and Amstel bock as they please" ; deplores Brarudi's poor communication and says it silently watches the illegal price increase of Amstel bock: "Brarudi is aware of this speculation. Its commercial representatives are in these bars, knowingly violating the fixed prices", calling on the company to punish the traders and representatives involved ; calls on consumers to report traders who do not respect Brarudi's set prices ; sounds the alarm: "The Ministry of Trade must get its act together to protect consumers against the speculation of certain traders."

a4392.speaker: Remy Ndayishimiye, spokesman for Brarudi
a4392.name: Remy Ndayishimiye
a4392.title: spokesman for Brarudi
a4392.speech: Asked for comment, declined to comment.

a4546.speaker: Executive Director of AFRYDEV, represented by Program Manager Edoka Ogwuche Abdullahi
a4546.name: Executive Director of AFRYDEV
a4546.title: represented by Program Manager Edoka Ogwuche Abdullahi
a4546.speech: In an overview of the workshop, emphasized the importance of a unified approach to protecting vulnerable populations and creating safer communities across the BAY states.

a4616.speaker: Some of the signees (House of Representatives members)
a4616.name: Some of the signees (House of Representatives members)
a4616.speech: Have already confessed to what appears to be a bribery.

a4616.speaker: Tiawan Saye Gongloe, Liberian human rights advocate and former presidential contender
a4616.name: Tiawan Saye Gongloe
a4616.title: Liberian human rights advocate and former presidential contender
a4616.speech: Has said individuals involved in accepting bribes on Capitol Hill as inducement to remove House Speaker Jonathan Fonati Koffa have directly undermined the principles of good governance and integrity essential for the nation's progress ; said Section 9.1 of the Code of Conduct explicitly forbids public officials from accepting bribes or gifts that could influence their professional responsibilities, adding that Section 12.50 of the Penal Law of Liberia categorizes bribery as a second-degree felony ; “If proven, these actions constitute a grave breach of public trust and a blatant violation of the law. Government is a place to serve, not to steal.” ; In a statement released to the public, commended a member of the House of Representatives who “exposed the unethical, unlawful, and criminal act of receiving US$15,000 in a conspiracy to remove the Speaker of the House of Representatives”, saying this act of bravery by the whistleblower exemplifies integrity and accountability in public service ; said the action by lawmaker Luther Collins aligns with his party Broom Movement's mission to eradicate corruption from the Government of Liberia, setting a commendable example for other lawmakers across Africa ; “The revelation of this conspiracy necessitates immediate and decisive action. Under Liberian law, specifically Chapter 9 of the Code of Conduct for Public Officials and Government Employees and Chapter 12 of the Penal Law, bribery is classified as a second-degree felony, punishable by up to five years of imprisonment. The law unequivocally prohibits any public servant from receiving, soliciting, or accepting bribes in exchange for official actions or for neglecting their duties.” ; is calling on the Ministry of Justice and the Liberia Anti-Corruption Commission to promptly initiate a thorough investigation into this matter and to prosecute those found culpable including both the receivers and the givers, to the fullest extent of the law ; “Bribery in government is not merely a crime; it is a profound betrayal of public trust. Moving forward, we must ensure that whistleblowers are both encouraged and protected, as they play a crucial role in exposing corruption and safeguarding our nation's integrity.” ; added that the fight against bribery and corruption is fundamental to building a more transparent and accountable Liberia ; “Together, we must steadfastly defend the integrity of our government institutions. This issue should not be ignored or concealed, as the betrayal of public trust has severe negative repercussions for our people.” ; said that considering each of the 48 Members of the House of Representatives received US$15,000, totaling US$720,000 or LD 136,800,000 under this criminal conspiracy, the magnitude of the act has subverted support for schools and clinics in desperate need of money.

a4616.speaker: Tiawan Saye Gongloe, Liberian human rights advocate and former presidential contender
a4616.name: Tiawan Saye Gongloe
a4616.title: Liberian human rights advocate and former presidential contender
a4616.speech: “This is one of the reasons I am advocating for the elimination of graduation fees from Kindergarten to the University level in both private and public schools.”

a4709.speaker: Emmerson Mnangagwa, President of Zimbabwe and Commander-In-Chief of the Zimbabwe Defence Forces
a4709.name: Emmerson Mnangagwa
a4709.title: President of Zimbabwe and Commander-In-Chief of the Zimbabwe Defence Forces
a4709.speech: Said the Southern African Development Community (SADC) region and Africa at large should scale up multi-pronged strategies to "Silence the Guns" on the continent, and that the astronomical cost of wars and conflicts deprive the people of much needed development and prosperity: "May I once again emphasise that Africa and our SADC region should scale up multi-pronged strategies to 'Silence The Guns' on our continent. The astronomical cost of wars and conflicts deprive our people, of the much needed development and prosperity. The SADC Mutual Defence Pact as well as the United Nation's Charter enjoin States to pursue the settlement of international disputes by peaceful means." ; Said it is imperative that due attention be given to equip officers with the essential know-how to promote the peaceful settlement of disputes through negotiation, conciliation, mediation or arbitration, for the benefit of the people.

a4709.speaker: Emmerson Mnangagwa, President of Zimbabwe
a4709.name: Emmerson Mnangagwa
a4709.title: President of Zimbabwe
a4709.speech: Said that in light of the growing negative impact of climate change, it is critically important that the relevant members of the defence forces constantly enhance capabilities around disaster management, adding that the efficient and timely co-ordination of both internal and regional humanitarian assistance in the aftermath of natural disasters should also be improved.

a4709.speaker: Emmerson Mnangagwa, President of Zimbabwe
a4709.name: Emmerson Mnangagwa
a4709.title: President of Zimbabwe
a4709.speech: Said security and defence infrastructure is of strategic and fundamental importance in the maintenance of national sovereignty and territorial integrity: "It is equally integral in advancing sustainable economic and social development, not only in our beloved motherland, Zimbabwe, but within the SADC region and African Continent as a whole."

a4709.speaker: Emmerson Mnangagwa, President of Zimbabwe
a4709.name: Emmerson Mnangagwa
a4709.title: President of Zimbabwe
a4709.speech: Deplored the broader security environment in the region which is characterised by armed conflicts, terrorism as well as the proliferation and illicit trafficking in small arms and light weapons; expressed concern over the increase in organised, transnational crime, drug trafficking, money laundering and human trafficking on the continent.

a4709.speaker: Emmerson Mnangagwa, President of Zimbabwe
a4709.name: Emmerson Mnangagwa
a4709.title: President of Zimbabwe
a4709.speech: Said technology advancements have resulted in greater discoveries of additional rich natural resources within Zimbabwe and on the continent, but regrettably this has entailed greater interests from those who would want to rob them by seeking to manipulate, coerce, infiltrate and even over-throw governments: "All these, among many others, call for defence and security training, skills and manpower development that speak to the challenges of this contemporary and diverse security environment. Additionally, there are various forms of asymmetrical warfare, undue interference in the internal affairs of our countries, monopolisation and manipulation of the global media space." ; Challenged members of the defence forces of Zimbabwe, SADC and Africa to continually enhance their capacity to prevent the subversion of their respective and collective constitutional order and national sovereignty.

a4732.speaker: Jens Hanefeld, German Ambassador to Ethiopia and Permanent Representative to the African Union
a4732.name: Jens Hanefeld
a4732.title: German Ambassador to Ethiopia and Permanent Representative to the African Union
a4732.speech: Dismissed talks that Europe's export powerhouse is in permanent decline; inflation, he noted, has eased to 2.1pc, even if growth is flat: "While Germany has indeed had a period of sluggish growth for the last three years, the rise in the cost of living is not that much of a problem at this point. We currently see an inflation rate of around 2.1pc, which is not overly alarming" ; "While the cost of living is naturally something to keep an eye on, I believe the bigger issue is economic growth" ; "We have a new government with a strong mandate for reform. Chancellor Friedrich Merz's statement this week outlined a very ambitious plan to address this, and I am optimistic that Germany will return to its traditional position as an economic powerhouse in Europe."

a4732.speaker: Jens Hanefeld, German Ambassador to Ethiopia and Permanent Representative to the African Union
a4732.name: Jens Hanefeld
a4732.title: German Ambassador to Ethiopia and Permanent Representative to the African Union
a4732.speech: Believes the new government under Chancellor Friedrich Merz's coalition has room to kick-start the economy by trimming the civil service by eight percent and unleashing "the Mittelstand," the small, specialised firms he credits for Germany's engineering edge; deregulation, not dirigisme, will restore Germany's lead in the European Union: "Germany has always very much relied on skills for its economic model. We do not have many natural resources in the sense of raw materials. We are dependent on open trade and open borders - engaging with the world - while fundamentally depending on the skills and expertise of our people" ; "One of Germany's particular economic strengths has always been its culture of small and medium enterprises (SMEs). These firms, sometimes known only within very specialised fields, often emerge as world leaders in their niches, particularly in machinery and, increasingly, new technologies" ; "What we now see, and what the new government has been adamant about, is a protracted policy of deregulation and cutting back on state intervention. Among the coalition's commitments is an eight percent reduction in the public sector over the coming four years, a strong signal that the government intends to allow the private sector the necessary breathing space for innovation."

a4732.speaker: Jens Hanefeld, German Ambassador to Ethiopia and Permanent Representative to the African Union
a4732.name: Jens Hanefeld
a4732.title: German Ambassador to Ethiopia and Permanent Representative to the African Union
a4732.speech: On why Germany is not a major trading partner of Ethiopia: "We should be careful when comparing across such a historical timeline. Ethiopia has undergone numerous political transitions, from monarchy to communist rule to its present system, each profoundly affecting the business climate" ; "Nonetheless, there is certainly room for improvement in foreign investment. Ethiopia has tremendous potential, particularly in green energy, where it can leverage abundant, CO-neutral power, something highly valued abroad and by Germany. Our task now is to work together to create a business environment that instils confidence in both foreign and domestic investors, ensuring they experience Ethiopia's reforms as credible and sustainable."

a4732.speaker: Jens Hanefeld, German Ambassador to Ethiopia and Permanent Representative to the African Union
a4732.name: Jens Hanefeld
a4732.title: German Ambassador to Ethiopia and Permanent Representative to the African Union
a4732.speech: Praised the government's "home-grown" reforms, from a new foreign-currency regime that lets investors repatriate dividends to broader macro fixes the IMF has welcomed: "The progress in macroeconomic reform - much more than liberalising the forex regime - has been truly impressive. The term 'homegrown economic reform' signals strong national ownership, and not something imposed from outside. From my conversations, there is widespread appreciation for the speed and commitment to these reforms. Of course, there is room for improvement, but maintaining the course is critical" ; "From our perspective, the system has been liberalised. We see how most banks adjust the exchange rate according to demand and offer. The fact that foreign companies can now transfer dividends out of Ethiopia demonstrates that the mechanism is functioning. It was understood from the outset that it would not operate flawlessly overnight. Nevertheless, I am impressed by its performance and echo the IMF's positive assessments."

a4732.speaker: Jens Hanefeld, German Ambassador to Ethiopia and Permanent Representative to the African Union
a4732.name: Jens Hanefeld
a4732.title: German Ambassador to Ethiopia and Permanent Representative to the African Union
a4732.speech: On development aid and the social cost of reform: development aid, re-routed during the northern war, is still flowing, he said, cushioning the pain of reforms and shoring up the Pretoria peace deal ; "Through our development cooperation, we also seek to alleviate any hardships these reforms might impose on parts of the population, reinforcing social stability alongside economic adjustment" ; "Let me clarify that we did not stop our development cooperation after the outbreak of the war but we shifted our efforts to support the Ethiopian people directly."

a4732.speaker: Jens Hanefeld, German Ambassador to Ethiopia and Permanent Representative to the African Union
a4732.name: Jens Hanefeld
a4732.title: German Ambassador to Ethiopia and Permanent Representative to the African Union
a4732.speech: On Ethiopia's peace and stability: "Germany values national reconciliation and a peaceful political system that includes all stakeholders. We fully support the Pretoria Agreement and commend Ethiopia's partners, including the African Union, for facilitating this peace framework" ; "Germany is committed to backing Ethiopia - politically and financially - through next year's elections, ensuring broad representation and internal stability" ; "I see many dedicated people working earnestly on reconciliation and peacebuilding. Conflict resolution is never easy, but commitment and dialogue are key" ; "Ethiopia's geopolitical role, hosting refugees and combating terrorism, demonstrates its constructive engagement. Staying the course on reconciliation and inclusive governance remains the only viable path forward."

a4732.speaker: Jens Hanefeld, German Ambassador to Ethiopia and Permanent Representative to the African Union
a4732.name: Jens Hanefeld
a4732.title: German Ambassador to Ethiopia and Permanent Representative to the African Union
a4732.speech: On transitional justice and accountability: "We believe in the importance of transitional justice and have consistently designated it as a key priority within our EU and bilateral support frameworks. Ultimately, Ethiopians must agree on and implement their own mechanisms for justice and reconciliation. We stand ready to support these efforts. The pace of transitional justice is a matter for domestic judgment, but from our view, there is room to accelerate processes without undermining local ownership."

a4732.speaker: Jens Hanefeld, German Ambassador to Ethiopia and Permanent Representative to the African Union
a4732.name: Jens Hanefeld
a4732.title: German Ambassador to Ethiopia and Permanent Representative to the African Union
a4732.speech: On migration and the EU visa delay: called the long waits for Ethiopian visa applicants to Europe a temporary European Union tool, improving cooperation on returning migrants ; "The Jobs Compact, which has come to an end, has largely achieved its initial goals, particularly in responding to the COVID crisis. We are cooperating closely with Ethiopian authorities on the longer-term migration management" ; "Germany believes in qualified, regulated migration rather than unregulated flows, we are designing frameworks that offer clear and legal pathways for skilled workers" ; "This is a European issue, not a bilateral one... The extended visa processing time - not an impediment to travel - reflects challenges in the return process for Ethiopians residing irregularly in Europe. Ethiopian authorities are taking steps to improve cooperation, and we are monitoring progress to ensure the measures remain temporary" ; "It is important to note that the delay does not reduce the number of visas issued; it only extends the processing time to 45 days. While I understand the inconvenience, we are seeing constructive steps from Ethiopian counterparts, and I expect the situation to normalise."

a4732.speaker: Jens Hanefeld, German Ambassador to Ethiopia and Permanent Representative to the African Union
a4732.name: Jens Hanefeld
a4732.title: German Ambassador to Ethiopia and Permanent Representative to the African Union
a4732.speech: On green energy and hydrogen: sees big promise in green energy, pointing to hydropower that could feed a global appetite for clean hydrogen ; "Germany's primary commitment is to reduce CO under the Paris Agreement. Hydrogen became a strategic focus after Russia weaponised energy supplies with its war of aggression against Ukraine. Ethiopia's hydropower success is remarkable because the green electricity share here is among the highest globally" ; "We support all renewable energy projects that reduce carbon emissions, respecting each country's sovereign choices while encouraging best practices" ; "Ultimately, each country makes its own energy decisions. Germany advocates global climate commitments and encourages partners to meet their CO targets. We provide technical and financial assistance where it aligns with these shared goals. Our role is to facilitate, not prescribe, respecting national sovereignty while promoting international cooperation."

a4732.speaker: Jens Hanefeld, German Ambassador to Ethiopia and Permanent Representative to the African Union
a4732.name: Jens Hanefeld
a4732.title: German Ambassador to Ethiopia and Permanent Representative to the African Union
a4732.speech: On the 2035 combustion-engine ban and the German car industry: "For probably a century, the German automotive industry has relied primarily on its engineering expertise in the construction of combustion engines. The shift towards emission-free mobility is obviously a challenge for a country that lacks raw materials" ; noted a combustion engine consists of up to 4,500 parts while an electric vehicle engine consists of less than 400 parts, making the transition a challenge for a raw-material-poor, engineering-based economy ; "I would not say that we see a crisis or anything but a transition, which is fundamental to a key industry in Germany. But at the same time, it is not as if the German industry is failing in this field, quite on the contrary. I am convinced that the German car industry will continue playing a very strong role in our industrial base" ; "German carmakers, while perhaps a little hesitant initially in adopting new technologies, have now wholeheartedly embraced them and are increasingly becoming world leaders in this field as well" ; "The 2035 combustion-engine ban is EU law. Member states must comply, and I am unaware of any plans to amend it. If adjustments become necessary, they will be debated within the EU framework. For now, all signs point to Germany meeting its legal commitments."

a4732.speaker: Jens Hanefeld, German Ambassador to Ethiopia and Permanent Representative to the African Union
a4732.name: Jens Hanefeld
a4732.title: German Ambassador to Ethiopia and Permanent Representative to the African Union
a4732.speech: On savings, finance and Germany's industrial base: "I think Germany has something like a 10pc savings rate. This puts us a lot higher than other countries, but we are not the highest. I think the savings rate is a stabilising factor in many ways, including domestic spending and expenditures, as well as the credit rating of the country as a whole" ; "The new government has made it clear that it intends to ensure regulations, which will incentivise increased investment by private investors. Given the financial requirements, we will also have to carefully follow what will happen to the international bond markets" ; "One of the things which we have definitely discovered, and I think we're not the only ones, is that a more traditional industrial base tends to provide very well-paying jobs. There is a strong interest everywhere in the world at this point in time to maintain this kind of employment, and I think Germany is well positioned for that" ; "Germany's model, rebuilt after World War II, has proven its resilience and adaptability, often quietly led by family-owned SMEs. This model delivers high-quality jobs and sustained competitiveness. While the service and digital sectors are growing, industry remains a cornerstone. A balanced economy that preserves strong manufacturing while embracing innovation reflects our national interest."

a4732.speaker: Jens Hanefeld, German Ambassador to Ethiopia and Permanent Representative to the African Union
a4732.name: Jens Hanefeld
a4732.title: German Ambassador to Ethiopia and Permanent Representative to the African Union
a4732.speech: On reunification lessons for Ethiopia: recalled that Germany merged NATO and Warsaw Pact forces after 1990, proving that adversaries can forge a single army when compromise is genuine ; "Germany, as a once divided country - which after all was on two sides during the Cold War - has learned quite a bit about national reconciliation and bringing people together, who have sometimes had very different experiences" ; "The German armed forces are a case in point because they integrated an army of the Warsaw Pact (the National People's Army of East Germany) and that of NATO (the Bundeswehr of West Germany) into one new united force" ; "National reconciliation is never easy; it is hard. You have to work for it, commit to it, and compromise. It will never work without these. Germany's experience showed genuine reconciliation requires commitment, compromise, and inclusive institutions."

a4732.speaker: Jens Hanefeld, German Ambassador to Ethiopia and Permanent Representative to the African Union
a4732.name: Jens Hanefeld
a4732.title: German Ambassador to Ethiopia and Permanent Representative to the African Union
a4732.speech: On conditionality, human rights and leverage: said Berlin prefers quiet persuasion to "megaphone diplomacy" on human rights, but it does expect progress on transitional justice, a freer press and credible elections ; "Our relationship with Ethiopia is built on open dialogue and mutual respect, not unilateral preconditions. We address sensitive issues through diplomatic channels, encouraging constructive solutions rather than public ultimatums. Maintaining trust and partnership is more effective than imposing rigid external demands. Also, almost all of our humanitarian and development support directly benefits the people of Ethiopia" ; "Ethiopia is a proud, independent nation with its own history and vision. Our influence is exercised through partnership and shared interests, not imposition. Diplomacy is about balancing respect for sovereignty with advocacy for common goals. True leverage comes from demonstrating value as a reliable partner in areas like development cooperation, trade, and investment."

a4732.speaker: Jens Hanefeld, German Ambassador to Ethiopia and Permanent Representative to the African Union
a4732.name: Jens Hanefeld
a4732.title: German Ambassador to Ethiopia and Permanent Representative to the African Union
a4732.speech: On his role and hopes for his tenure: "To be honest, nothing keeps me awake. All the interlocutors I have met are deeply committed to Ethiopia's future. My hope is that Ethiopia continues to play a constructive role internationally at a time when the rules-based order faces challenges. Ensuring peace, stability, and a thriving economy will allow Ethiopia's voice to be heard as a force for good" ; "As a German diplomat, I am a civil servant, a career officer, and not a political appointee. I see my role essentially as serving the bilateral relationship between Germany and Ethiopia... I do not see myself as the figurehead of change, but rather as an enabler, someone who provides support and sometimes guidance in the background" ; "I would be happy if the bilateral relationship between Germany and Ethiopia continued to thrive... I hope we will have proceeded further on Ethiopia's path toward economic reform, building on the important steps taken last summer. I want to look back then on a flourishing cooperation in the field of culture and education; just to mention that the German Embassy school, where many Ethiopian children receive excellent education, is turning 70 this year" ; "One of the most significant achievements I would point to is national reconciliation and peace, which provide the groundwork for a prosperous future aligned with ongoing reforms. I also hope to see progress in the rule of law, transitional justice, and freedom of the press, issues that are crucial for sustainable development and international confidence."

a4732.speaker: Friedrich Merz, German Chancellor
a4732.name: Friedrich Merz
a4732.title: German Chancellor
a4732.speech: His statement this week outlined a very ambitious plan to address Germany's economic growth problem.

a4732.speaker: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
a4732.name: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
a4732.speech: Has welcomed Ethiopia's broader macroeconomic fixes and given positive assessments of the liberalised foreign-exchange regime.

a4768.speaker: International AIDS Society (IAS)
a4768.name: International AIDS Society (IAS)
a4768.speech: Has hailed a bipartisan move by the United States Senate to shield the President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) from proposed budget cuts amounting to USD 400 million, outlined in President Donald Trump's rescission package.

a4768.speaker: Beatriz Grinsztejn, IAS President
a4768.name: Beatriz Grinsztejn
a4768.title: IAS President
a4768.speech: Described PEPFAR as “one of the greatest success stories in global health” ; “Global advocacy played a crucial role in persuading US lawmakers to protect this vital programme, reminding them that decisions about PEPFAR shape the health and futures of people around the world. Yet uncertainty remains, with ongoing threats to global health funding. We must stay vigilant.”

a4768.speaker: Kenneth Ngure, IAS President-Elect
a4768.name: Kenneth Ngure
a4768.title: IAS President-Elect
a4768.speech: Underscored the programme's significance to the African continent, calling PEPFAR “a lifeline for communities across Africa,” and insisted that African leadership must be central to the conversation: “We need to keep advancing discussions about sustainable financing – including stronger domestic investments and strategies to reduce dependence on global donors.”

a4768.speaker: International AIDS Society (IAS)
a4768.name: International AIDS Society (IAS)
a4768.speech: Urged swift and decisive action to protect essential HIV services and appealed to global leaders to maintain robust investment in programmes that save lives, promote health equity, and support long-term development.

a5002.speaker: Dr. Diaka Sidibe, Guinean Minister of Commerce
a5002.name: Dr. Diaka Sidibe
a5002.title: Guinean Minister of Commerce
a5002.speech: Stressed that the DDI/DDE service plays a key role in improving the efficiency and transparency of commercial operations, thereby strengthening the competitiveness of the Guinean economy.

a5002.speaker: Dr. Diaka Sidibe, Guinean Minister of Commerce
a5002.name: Dr. Diaka Sidibe
a5002.title: Guinean Minister of Commerce
a5002.speech: Acknowledged that, although Guinea signed the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) agreement in 2018 and put in place several initiatives to facilitate trade, additional efforts are needed to enable young people, women and SMEs to take full advantage of the opportunities offered by this agreement; with this in mind, she mentioned the creation of an improved digital platform aimed at making the ministry's services faster, more accessible and of better quality, while encouraging the formalisation of informal businesses.

a5002.speaker: Director of the Import and Export Descriptive Declarations Service (DDI/DDE)
a5002.name: Director of the Import and Export Descriptive Declarations Service (DDI/DDE)
a5002.speech: Addressed the challenges encountered since he took office in March 2022, in particular the transition to fully digitalised management; although this development is promising, it has revealed shortcomings in terms of staff training and support, so a partnership with the UNDP was sought to draw up a strategic plan responding to the new challenges.

a5002.speaker: Representative of the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP)
a5002.name: Representative of the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP)
a5002.speech: Reaffirmed his organisation's commitment to supporting Guinea in its socio-economic development efforts; he also insisted on the need to improve the business climate and to fully integrate young people and women into intra-African trade, notably through the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA).

a5012.speaker: Nandita Murukutla, Vice President of Global Policy and Research, Vital Strategies
a5012.name: Nandita Murukutla
a5012.title: Vice President of Global Policy and Research, Vital Strategies
a5012.speech: Giving an in-depth overview of the report ‘The Sobering Truth: Incentivizing Alcohol Death and Disability’, expressed that economic incentives may sound like a good thing, but aren’t always good for everyone involved, more so when the incentivized “actions” contribute to the death of 3 million people per year: “They become, in the words of economists, ‘perverse.’ This report-the first of its kind-lifts the lid on the significant economic incentives that governments and international development agencies give to the alcohol industry, even though the industry has a well-known postmortem record of causing death and harm... It is, therefore, utterly mind-boggling, given the huge toll of death and disability, that high-level global development agencies would incentivize countries to give financial breaks to the perpetrator-the alcohol industry-under the guise of development assistance.”

a5012.speaker: Nandita Murukutla, Vice President of Global Policy and Research, Vital Strategies
a5012.name: Nandita Murukutla
a5012.title: Vice President of Global Policy and Research, Vital Strategies
a5012.speech: On the report’s findings about development aid: “The Sobering Truth: Incentivizing Alcohol Death and Disability reviews publicly available data on economic incentives going to the alcohol industry over the past 25 years from governments and development agencies. We find that significant investments, including development aid intended for the welfare and growth of those societies, are most often allocated in low- and middle-income countries for the production and promotion of alcohol, a product that is well-known to cause extensive death and disability. Governments, the development community and concerned citizens need to reexamine the current economic incentives to the alcohol industry. There’s a contradiction between the stated intent of the public spending, which is meant for the economic development and welfare of societies, and the reality of its use. These less-resourced recipient countries identified in our report have among the highest alcohol burdens in their societies, including the highest attributable deaths from alcohol.”

a5012.speaker: Nandita Murukutla, Vice President of Global Policy and Research, Vital Strategies
a5012.name: Nandita Murukutla
a5012.title: Vice President of Global Policy and Research, Vital Strategies
a5012.speech: On alcohol advertising: “The marketing, promotion and sponsorship of alcohol is one of the chief drivers of the growing rates of alcohol consumption worldwide. And yet, the advertising of alcohol continues unabated. Even worse, alcohol companies can claim tax deductions on their marketing budgets in some countries... It is indeed shameful that a single multinational corporation’s budget for advertising should rival public expenditures for health in all low-income countries... There is no room or economic justification for diverting public incentives towards a product that is contributing to more than 3 million deaths each year.”

a5012.speaker: Nandita Murukutla, Vice President of Global Policy and Research, Vital Strategies
a5012.name: Nandita Murukutla
a5012.title: Vice President of Global Policy and Research, Vital Strategies
a5012.speech: On FIFA World Cup tax waivers: “FIFA, the international governing body for football, requires a host country to give tax breaks on any profits made by its commercial partners, including alcohol producer AB InBev. While the tax breaks allow AB InBev to reap substantial profits, it deprives the host country of millions in revenue that could have been used to improve the health and well-being of its people. During the 2014 World Cup, FIFA required the host country Brazil to give tax breaks to FIFA, AB InBev and other commercial partners, totaling US $475 million... In 2010, South Africa hosted the World Cup, and FIFA, AB InBev and other commercial partners reported receiving US $3.8 billion tax-free in revenue. However, South Africa experienced a $3.1 billion net loss from hosting the event.”

a5012.speaker: Nandita Murukutla, Vice President of Global Policy and Research, Vital Strategies
a5012.name: Nandita Murukutla
a5012.title: Vice President of Global Policy and Research, Vital Strategies
a5012.speech: On beer companies subsidising seed production in Africa: “So many more lives are harmed than are helped with these incentives to the alcohol industry. The Sobering Truth... highlights an example of this in Uganda, when global alcohol producer SABMiller leveraged a production subsidy of a local seed variety for beer production to encourage local farmers to produce and harvest it... Yet, the incentive also promoted the growth and sale of beer in Uganda, a country where alcohol use is the leading risk factor for premature death. While governments have a responsibility towards their citizens to grow domestic economies, our report urges governments to do so in a manner that is sustainable and that will reap long-term benefits.”

a5013.speaker: Financial Times (British newspaper)
a5013.name: Financial Times (British newspaper)
a5013.speech: Reports a growing shortage of uranium in the West, allegedly caused by the actions of Russia and China; that Kazakhstan, the world's largest uranium producer (40% of world output), has considerably reduced its supplies to Western markets while increasing exports to Russia and China.

a5013.speaker: Unnamed experts
a5013.name: Unnamed experts
a5013.speech: Note the growing gap between Western countries' desire to secure the safety of uranium supply and their plans to increase the use of nuclear energy.

a5026.speaker: International Organization for Migration (IOM)
a5026.name: International Organization for Migration (IOM)
a5026.speech: Launched an appeal for USD 77.6 million to provide humanitarian assistance to more than 1.2 million internally displaced persons (IDPs), returnees, host community members and migrants in Ethiopia.

a5026.speaker: Ester Ruiz de Azua, IOM Ethiopia’s Emergency and Post-Crisis Programme Coordinator
a5026.name: Ester Ruiz de Azua
a5026.title: IOM Ethiopia’s Emergency and Post-Crisis Programme Coordinator
a5026.speech: “IOM Ethiopia plans to provide support following two principal objectives: saving lives while responding to the humanitarian crisis and supporting the transition and recovery of crisis-affected communities.”

a5048.speaker: International Monetary Fund (April 2025 Regional Economic Outlook for Sub-Saharan Africa)
a5048.name: International Monetary Fund (April 2025 Regional Economic Outlook for Sub-Saharan Africa)
a5048.speech: Urged that the private sector must take a leading role in Ghana's long-term economic growth as global funding conditions tighten, saying countries like Ghana would increasingly need to depend on private sector innovation and investment to meet their development goals as official development assistance and concessional financing are expected to decline: "With external funding conditions becoming more constrained, the burden of achieving long-term development targets will increasingly fall on domestic private sectors."

a5048.speaker: International Monetary Fund (April 2025 Regional Economic Outlook for Sub-Saharan Africa)
a5048.name: International Monetary Fund (April 2025 Regional Economic Outlook for Sub-Saharan Africa)
a5048.speech: Noted that while Ghana had made progress in stabilising its macroeconomic environment, sustained growth would require structural reforms aimed at improving the business climate, supporting trade integration, and attracting private investment ; stressed the need to strengthen governance, invest in infrastructure, and develop human capital to create an environment in which the private sector can thrive.

a5048.speaker: International Monetary Fund (April 2025 Regional Economic Outlook for Sub-Saharan Africa)
a5048.name: International Monetary Fund (April 2025 Regional Economic Outlook for Sub-Saharan Africa)
a5048.speech: Observed that nearly one-third of the population of sub-Saharan Africa, including Ghana's vulnerable groups, still lives below the international poverty line, and warned that without strong private sector-led growth, efforts to reduce poverty could be undermined.

a5048.speaker: International Monetary Fund (April 2025 Regional Economic Outlook for Sub-Saharan Africa)
a5048.name: International Monetary Fund (April 2025 Regional Economic Outlook for Sub-Saharan Africa)
a5048.speech: Called for greater mobilisation of domestic revenues and improved spending discipline to support important sectors and promote inclusive development.

a5170.speaker: Abebe Selassie, Director of the IMF's African Department
a5170.name: Abebe Selassie
a5170.title: Director of the IMF's African Department
a5170.speech: Sought to understand the Government's reform priorities and commitment to maintaining sound macroeconomic management.

a5170.speaker: Joseph Mwanamvekha, Malawi Minister of Finance, Economic Planning and Development
a5170.name: Joseph Mwanamvekha
a5170.title: Malawi Minister of Finance, Economic Planning and Development
a5170.speech: Reaffirmed President Arthur Peter Mutharika's commitment to fiscal discipline and stability. He said: “Government has already started implementing measures aimed at cutting unnecessary external and internal travel, promoting virtual meetings, and advancing talks with development partners to restructure debt and ease fiscal pressures.”

a5170.speaker: Eric Meyer, Deputy Assistant Secretary for Africa and the Middle East, U.S. Department of the Treasury
a5170.name: Eric Meyer
a5170.title: Deputy Assistant Secretary for Africa and the Middle East, U.S. Department of the Treasury
a5170.speech: Reaffirmed Washington's support for Malawi despite current global economic headwinds. Acknowledged the impact of post-USAID funding cuts, particularly in the health sector, but expressed optimism about the revival of U.S. development programmes. He said discussions are underway with the Global Health team to explore renewed support for Malawi's fight against HIV and AIDS, tuberculosis, and related diseases.

a5170.speaker: Eric Meyer, Deputy Assistant Secretary for Africa and the Middle East, U.S. Department of the Treasury
a5170.name: Eric Meyer
a5170.title: Deputy Assistant Secretary for Africa and the Middle East, U.S. Department of the Treasury
a5170.speech: Advised the Malawi Government to maintain close engagement with the IMF on debt management and sustainability, describing it as key to unlocking investment and development opportunities ; noted the untapped potential in Malawi's mining sector, saying that while many investors have shown interest, progress has been hampered by inconsistent regulations and persistent energy challenges.

a5170.speaker: Joseph Mwanamvekha, Malawi Minister of Finance, Economic Planning and Development
a5170.name: Joseph Mwanamvekha
a5170.title: Malawi Minister of Finance, Economic Planning and Development
a5170.speech: Thanked the U.S. Government for its continued partnership and reaffirmed Malawi's readiness to work closely with the IMF and other partners. He said the government is implementing reforms designed to make Malawi an attractive investment destination, particularly in the mining and other productive sectors, through regulatory reforms and improvements to the business environment.

a5241.speaker: Emmanuel Hanai, Chairman of the Tanzania Environmental Experts Association (TEEA)
a5241.name: Emmanuel Hanai
a5241.title: Chairman of the Tanzania Environmental Experts Association (TEEA)
a5241.speech: said on December 13, 2024, at the association's sixth general meeting, that 65 companies registered by the National Environment Management Council (NEMC) in 2021 have been unable to work because of shortcomings in the 2021 Regulations on the registration and operation of environmental experts ; "In 2021, NEMC registered 65 companies to carry out environmental impact assessments (EIA), but after the implementation of this regulation, to date there is no company that can continue working under the requirement of this regulation" ; said TEEA, NEMC and those companies have already begun discussions on the best way to ensure they continue providing services to the community without harming investors, investment and operations in general.

a5241.speaker: Emmanuel Hanai, Chairman of the Tanzania Environmental Experts Association (TEEA)
a5241.name: Emmanuel Hanai
a5241.title: Chairman of the Tanzania Environmental Experts Association (TEEA)
a5241.speech: said another challenge they have submitted regarding the regulation concerns the removal of environmental consultants who are also public servants from carrying out EIA work ; "That has affected institutions such as those of higher education, where consultancy work is one of their normal duties and is in accordance with the University Charter."

a5241.speaker: Emmanuel Hanai, Chairman of the Tanzania Environmental Experts Association (TEEA)
a5241.name: Emmanuel Hanai
a5241.title: Chairman of the Tanzania Environmental Experts Association (TEEA)
a5241.speech: named another challenge as the low level of understanding among various stakeholders about the EIA guideline, with some government institutions and various stakeholders still implementing projects without carrying out environmental impact assessments ; "We consultants, in our work, witness the existence of many projects being run without EIA certificates or audits, and even some of those that have EIA and audits still do not implement the management directives as issued in the EIA reports and in the certificates themselves" ; said this situation has caused environmental degradation, including indiscriminate dumping of waste.

a5241.speaker: Emmanuel Hanai, Chairman of the Tanzania Environmental Experts Association (TEEA)
a5241.name: Emmanuel Hanai
a5241.title: Chairman of the Tanzania Environmental Experts Association (TEEA)
a5241.speech: said regarding the challenge of some industries and projects not employing environmental experts, that this challenge puts the environmental profession — which is recognised in the sustainable development of the world economy — at risk and causes an increase in environmental impacts including drought, floods, extreme heat and extreme cold.

a5241.speaker: Emmanuel Hanai, Chairman of the Tanzania Environmental Experts Association (TEEA)
a5241.name: Emmanuel Hanai
a5241.title: Chairman of the Tanzania Environmental Experts Association (TEEA)
